GEASS: Training-Free Caption Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Vision-Language Models

Zeshang Li Affiliation: University of International Relations, Beijing, China Correspondence to: zeshang.li@uir.edu.cn    Shuoyang Zhang Affiliation: University of International Relations, Beijing, China    Jiashen Ding Affiliation: Anhui University, Hefei, China
Abstract

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at grounded reasoning but remain prone to object hallucination. Recent work treats self-generated captions as a uniformly positive resource, yet we find that naively embedding one can degrade rather than help—dropping Qwen2.5-VL-3B accuracy on HallusionBench by nearly 1010 points. Two structural properties explain this. First, captions anchor not only the model’s final answer but also its reasoning trajectory and lexical choices. Second, caption errors are asymmetric: omissions vastly outnumber fabrications, yet each fabrication carries a much larger per-instance impact. A caption’s usefulness is therefore a per-query property, not a per-corpus one. We propose GEASS (Gated Evidence-Aware Selective Steering), a training-free module that decides on each query how much of the caption the model consumes: it gates the caption by the clean path’s confidence, weights it by the entropy reduction it produces, and raises the evidence bar when the two pathways disagree. Experiments on POPE and HallusionBench across four VLMs show that GEASS consistently improves over vanilla inference and contrastive decoding, with only two extra forward passes per query.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Wang et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b) have achieved remarkable progress on tasks such as visual question answering and grounded reasoning. However, VLMs suffer from a persistent failure known as object hallucination—generating responses inconsistent with the actual image content (Li et al., 2023; Augustin et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2024)—which undermines their reliability in scenarios where factual grounding is critical.

A key origin of this failure is the model’s query-driven attention pattern: when answering a specific question, VLMs focus locally and often fail to integrate evidence outside the question’s immediate scope (Huang et al., 2024; Tu et al., 2026). To address this limitation, two routes have emerged. The first route operates within the model, either refining training data and objectives (Liu et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024) or modifying the decoding process via contrastive decoding (Leng et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025) and attention reweighting (Tu et al., 2026). However, such methods redistribute the use of information already attended to but introduce no new visual evidence, and thus cannot recover what the model never observed. The second route therefore introduces external information through image captions, which are generated under a generic “describe this image” instruction and globally surface content that query-driven attention misses (Hu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024a; Kapuriya et al., 2025). However, these works uniformly treat captions as a positive auxiliary resource and feed them into the model unconditionally, leaving an open question: when, and to what extent, should a caption actually be trusted?

The cost of unconditional trust is concrete. We observe that naively embedding a self-generated caption drops Qwen2.5-VL-3B (Bai et al., 2025) accuracy on HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024)from 61.19 to 51.31 (Table 1)—a near 10-point degradation from a resource intended to help. The root cause is that captions are neither uniformly useful nor uniformly harmful but mixed-quality signals: captions are strong on global content and weak on details, while the model’s own answering is the opposite—so captions help on globally-oriented questions where they cover the model’s blind spot, but mislead on detail-oriented questions where their own omissions become the dominant error. Under such a background, a question naturally arises: can we adaptively decide how much a caption should influence the model on each query, at inference time and without additional training?

To answer this question, we investigate how captions actually shape VLM behavior, and obtain two observations explained in detail in Section 3.

  • •

    Captions exert a strong anchoring effect: once embedded, they reshape not only the final answer but also the model’s chain-of-thought, word choices, and syntax (Figure 1). Anchoring is content-neutral—it amplifies caption content faithfully whether or not that content is correct—which means the influence of a caption must be modulated rather than passively accepted.

  • •

    Caption errors, when they occur, are structurally asymmetric: the saliency-weighted global scan that gives captions their breadth also makes them omit small, peripheral, or occluded objects far more often than fabricate. The per-instance impact of the two error types is asymmetric as well—fabrication is rare but each occurrence is highly damaging, while omission is mild per instance but pervasive—and their combined effect is what produces the near 10-point drop in Table 1. Any inference-time mechanism consuming captions must therefore address both failure modes.

These observations expose a clear gap in existing approaches. Internal-intervention methods built on contrastive decoding assume the auxiliary input is uniformly degraded and should be subtracted away, which is mismatched with captions whose content is partly useful and partly missing. Caption-quality methods, in turn, do produce better captions—but always at a price: stronger captioners, external verification tools, or human curation, all of which incur substantial additional inference-time cost and still leave a residual gap that anchoring will amplify. The route that has not been explored is the cheapest one: leaving the caption as it is, and instead deciding—at inference time, on each query—how much of it the model should consume. A mechanism that operates at this level is orthogonal to caption-quality improvements, free of the overhead they carry, and directly addresses the mixed-quality nature of any realistic caption.

Inspired by these findings, we propose GEASS (Gated Evidence-Aware Selective Steering), a training-free module that adaptively regulates how much a caption is allowed to influence the model at the logit level, rather than altering the caption itself. GEASS runs two parallel forward passes—with and without the caption—and decides, on each query, the extent to which the caption may exert its influence through three signals, each operationalizing one judgment derived from our observations: (i) a confidence gate (Gated), derived from the clean-path maximum probability, proxies whether the answering pathway needs external help in the first place; (ii) an information-gain weight (Evidence-Aware), measured by the caption-induced entropy reduction, proxies whether the caption is actually delivering useful information for the current query; (iii) a disagreement penalty (Selective) raises the evidence threshold when the two paths disagree, encoding the omission-over-fabrication prior so that a caption is granted greater authority to reinforce the model’s judgment than to overturn it. GEASS is plug-and-play, requires no architectural modification, and adds only two extra forward passes per query. It applies to any VLM that exposes logits during decoding and is compatible with standard decoding strategies.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Caption-aided VLM inference is governed by two structural properties. We investigate how captions shape VLM behavior and identify the anchoring effect and the omission-dominated error asymmetry as the two properties that jointly determine when a caption helps and when it harms.

  • •

    GEASS: adaptive fusion for mixed-quality captions. Rather than altering the caption, GEASS selectively modulates its influence at the logit level through three signals, each a computable proxy for one identified property, retaining the benefits of accurate captions while suppressing the harms of flawed ones with nearly zero extra overhead.

  • •

    Plug-and-play capability and broad applicability. GEASS is validated on POPE and HallusionBench across four VLMs spanning different architectures and scales, achieving consistent gains over both vanilla inference and contrastive decoding baselines.

2 Related Work

2.1 Hallucination Mitigation in VLMs

Object hallucination—where VLMs (Liu et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024b) produce fluent but visually ungrounded content—has been documented across benchmarks targeting different aspects of the failure: yes/no polling on object existence (Li et al., 2023), hallucinated object ratios in free-form generation (Rohrbach et al., 2018), and large-vocabulary stress tests (Augustin et al., 2025). Mitigation efforts split along training and inference axes. On the training side, prior work has curated targeted data (Liu et al., 2023) or applied RLHF (Sun et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024), all of which improve robustness at the cost of substantial compute and supervision. Inference-time methods avoid retraining and intervene at decoding. One line leverages external vision models for post-hoc verification (Yin et al., 2024); a second reweights visual features to retain information that would otherwise be lost (Tu et al., 2026; Tong et al., 2024); a third—and the line most relevant to ours—operates at the logit level, contrasting the model’s output against a deliberately degraded counterpart. VCD (Leng et al., 2024) contrasts the original image against a noise-corrupted version to suppress language-prior tokens; OPERA (Huang et al., 2024) penalizes over-trust on summary tokens during beam search; recent work further refines the contrastive signal through internal-fact comparison (Wang et al., 2025), retrieval-augmented contrast (Lee & Song, 2025), head-level suppression (Sarkar et al., 2025), selective decoding (Park et al., 2025), and visual information steering (Li et al., 2025).

What unites this last line is a single assumption: the auxiliary input being contrasted is uniformly degraded, and its influence should be subtracted away. This assumption breaks down when the auxiliary input is itself partly informative—a setting we examine next.

2.2 Captions as Auxiliary Information in VLMs

Image captions are a natural way to inject the global view that query-driven attention misses, and have been used as auxiliary text across a range of VLM pipelines: as textual connectors for black-box LLMs in knowledge-based VQA (Hu et al., 2023), as filtered summaries that reduce noise before downstream consumption (Zhang et al., 2025), as higher-quality supervision during instruction tuning (Chen et al., 2024a), and as caption-aware fine-tuning for scientific VQA (Kapuriya et al., 2025). The shared premise across these works is that caption quality is the lever to pull: with a better captioner or a better filter, downstream performance follows.

Two questions are conspicuously absent from this literature. First, none of these works asks how captions interact with the model’s own reasoning once embedded—whether their effect is bounded by information provision, or whether the model’s outputs become entangled with the caption’s phrasing. Second, none asks what kinds of errors captions introduce, and whether different error types damage downstream performance asymmetrically. Our analysis in Section 3 shows that both questions have non-trivial answers, and that ignoring them is what makes naive caption augmentation backfire.

3 Preliminary Analysis

We investigate how captions actually shape VLM behavior, and identify two structural properties that jointly govern caption-aided inference: a deep anchoring effect (§3.2) and an asymmetric error structure (§3.4). Together they expose three failure modes that any inference-time mechanism consuming captions must address (§3.5).

3.1 Setup

We use Qwen2.5-VL-3B (Bai et al., 2025) as our primary model, with cross-validation on InternVL2-8B (Chen et al., 2024b), InternVL3-3.8B (Zhu et al., 2025), and a reasoning-augmented variant Qwen2.5-VL-3B†. Captions are produced by the model itself under the instruction “Describe this image in detail” with greedy decoding, and embedded as text below the original image to form a composite input fed back to the model alongside the question. Evaluation is performed on HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024) and COCO validation (Lin et al., 2014).

3.2 The Anchoring Effect

Once a caption is embedded into the input, its influence extends well beyond the final answer. In Figure 1, the model reasons correctly without the caption but, once the caption is provided, lifts phrases such as “the outlet is now glowing and ready to supply power” nearly verbatim into its chain-of-thought, and flips its answer accordingly. The pattern holds at scale: across 100 random HallusionBench samples, unigram, bigram, and trigram overlap with the caption rises sharply for all four models tested (Table 2).

The mechanism cuts both ways. Figure 3 shows the same image paired with two captions: a correct one (“a dog sitting on the beach”) leads both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and InternVL2-8B to revise an initially wrong No into Yes, while a fabricated one (“a cat…”) drives the same two models to flip in the same direction and invent supporting details. Anchoring does not distinguish between truth and error—the caption decides the direction, and Table 1 reflects the cost when the direction is wrong: naively embedding self-generated captions drops Qwen2.5-VL-3B accuracy on HallusionBench from 61.19 to 51.31. The influence of a caption must therefore be explicitly modulated rather than passively accepted.

3.3 Captions as Auxiliary Information in VLMs

3.4 Asymmetry of Caption Errors

Anchoring explains why caption errors propagate, but not which errors a caption is likely to make. To answer the latter, we compare objects mentioned in self-generated captions against ground-truth annotations on 500 COCO validation images, separating omissions (objects present but unmentioned) from fabrications (objects mentioned but absent). Across all four models, omissions outnumber fabrications by roughly X:1X{:}1 (Table 3), and the gap is concentrated on small, peripheral, and occluded objects (Figure 2). This is not random failure but a structural property of how captions are produced: a saliency-weighted global scan, prompted under a generic description instruction, naturally drops low-salience content, while a description task offers no incentive to invent.

Per-instance impact, however, runs in the opposite direction. Across 100 paired instances (Figure 4), fabrication shifts the prediction toward the wrong answer by Δ​p¯=0.64\overline{\Delta p}=0.64 on average and flips the binary decision in 87%87\% of cases; omission shifts it by only Δ​p¯=0.13\overline{\Delta p}=0.13 and flips 11%11\%. Fabrication is rare but each occurrence is near-fatal; omission is mild per instance but pervasive: multiple objects are typically dropped from a single caption, and the omission distribution, though centered near zero, retains a long tail that reaches the flip threshold. Neither error type alone could produce the 10-point drop in Table 1; the two accumulate through distinct channels—a few fabrications, each large, plus many omissions, each small.

The asymmetry has a direct design consequence: a caption’s reliability is not uniformly distributed across its text. Its positive assertions are highly trustworthy, while its silences carry little evidential weight. When the two pathways disagree—a caption attempting to overturn the model’s own judgment—the more likely culprit is a fabrication on the caption side, not an omission on the model side.

3.5 Design Implications

§3.2–§3.4 together expose three failure modes a caption-aided system can fall into on any given query: (i) the model is already correct on its own, and any caption influence—accurate or not—introduces noise; (ii) the caption fabricates, conflicting with the model and, by virtue of fabrication’s high per-instance impact, reversing a correct answer; (iii) the caption is dominated by omission and carries no information relevant to the current question, yet still leaks into the output through anchoring. The three modes have non-overlapping behavioral signatures—the model does not need help, the two pathways disagree and the caption side carries asymmetric risk, the caption fails to reduce model uncertainty—and can be distinguished by three query-specific proxies: the model’s prediction confidence, the caption-induced entropy reduction, and the agreement between the two pathways. We instantiate these proxies as the three components of GEASS in the next section.

4 Method

The three failure modes in Section 3.5 share a common structure: each is characterised by a distinct combination of two quantities the model exposes at decoding time—its own confidence on the clean path, and the change induced by the caption on top of it. We turn this observation into a method. GEASS performs two forward passes per query, with and without the caption, and combines their logits with a query-specific weight built from three components: a confidence gate that controls whether the caption is consulted at all, an information-gain term that measures how much the caption sharpens the prediction, and a disagreement penalty that raises the bar when the caption tries to override the model. The pipeline is shown in Figure 5.

4.1 Dual-Path Inference

Caption CC is produced by the same VLM under the prompt “Describe this image in detail” with greedy decoding, fixed once per image. At decoding step tt, two logit vectors are obtained:

𝐳clean(t)\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{\text{clean}}^{(t)} =fθ(⋅∣I,Q,y<t),\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid I,Q,y_{<t}), (1)
𝐳cap(t)\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{\text{cap}}^{(t)} =fθ(⋅∣I,Q,C,y<t),\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid I,Q,C,y_{<t}), (2)

where y<ty_{<t} are the tokens generated so far. The clean path is the model’s own answer in the absence of the caption; the caption path is the answer the model would give if it accepted CC at face value. The shift 𝐳cap(t)−𝐳clean(t)\mathbf{z}_{\text{cap}}^{(t)}-\mathbf{z}_{\text{clean}}^{(t)} isolates the caption’s contribution, and the rest of this section specifies how much of this shift to keep.

4.2 Confidence Gate

The first failure mode—the model is already correct—requires the caption to step aside whenever the clean path is decisive. We use the maximum probability of the clean distribution as a confidence proxy,

c(t)=maxv∈𝒱⁡pclean(t)​(v),pclean(t)=softmax⁡(𝐳clean(t)),c^{(t)}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\,p_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}(v),\quad p_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}=\mathrm{softmax}\big(\mathbf{z}_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}\big), (3)

which lies in (0,1](0,1] and is comparable across vocabularies and model scales. A sigmoid gate maps it to a fusion coefficient,

α(t)=σ⁡(−β⁡(c(t)−τ)),\alpha^{(t)}=\sigma\!\big(-\beta(c^{(t)}-\tau)\big), (4)

with threshold τ\tau and sharpness β\beta. The gate is closed (α→0\alpha\!\to\!0) when c(t)≫τc^{(t)}\!\gg\!\tau and open (α→1\alpha\!\to\!1) when c(t)≪τc^{(t)}\!\ll\!\tau; near τ\tau it interpolates smoothly. We set β\beta large enough that the transition occupies a narrow band around τ\tau, so the gate behaves as a soft switch rather than a continuous re-weighting.

4.3 Evidence-Aware Weighting

An open gate exposes the model to the caption but does not yet decide whether the caption deserves to be heard. The two remaining failure modes—fabrication and omission—are distinguished by what the caption does to the model’s distribution. We capture this with two terms.

Information gain.

A caption that carries query-relevant content sharpens the prediction; a caption that does not, leaves the distribution unchanged or makes it more diffuse. We measure this with relative entropy reduction,

r(t)=H⁡(pclean(t))−H⁡(pcap(t))H⁡(pclean(t))+ϵ,r^{(t)}=\frac{H\big(p_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}\big)-H\big(p_{\text{cap}}^{(t)}\big)}{H\big(p_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}\big)+\epsilon}, (5)

with H(p)=−∑vp(v)logp(v)H(p)=-\sum_{v}p(v)\log p(v) and a small ϵ\epsilon for stability. r(t)>0r^{(t)}\!>\!0 means the caption sharpens the model’s belief; r(t)≤0r^{(t)}\!\leq\!0 means it adds noise.

Disagreement penalty.

Information gain is symmetric: it does not distinguish a caption that reinforces the clean prediction from one that overturns it. The asymmetry established in Section 3.4 is exactly that these two cases should be treated differently—disagreement is more often produced by fabrication on the caption side than by omission on the model side. We encode this with an indicator,

a(t)=[argmaxpclean(t)=argmaxpcap(t)],a^{(t)}=\mathbbm{1}\!\Big[\arg\max p_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}=\arg\max p_{\text{cap}}^{(t)}\Big], (6)

and combine it with r(t)r^{(t)} into a single weight,

w(t)=σ⁡(η​r(t)−λ⁡(1−a(t))).w^{(t)}=\sigma\!\big(\eta\,r^{(t)}-\lambda(1-a^{(t)})\big). (7)

Under agreement (a(t)=1a^{(t)}\!=\!1) the penalty vanishes and w(t)w^{(t)} reduces to a sigmoid of scaled information gain. Under disagreement (a(t)=0a^{(t)}\!=\!0) the caption must compensate for the penalty: the break-even point w(t)=12w^{(t)}\!=\!\tfrac{1}{2} is reached only when r(t)≥λ/ηr^{(t)}\geq\lambda/\eta, so the ratio λ/η\lambda/\eta sets the minimum relative entropy reduction required for an override. With our defaults η=5,λ=2\eta=5,\lambda=2 this break-even sits at a 40%40\% reduction, separating informative corrections (large rr) from low-information disagreements (small rr) without requiring any per-query tuning.

4.4 Logit Fusion

The two terms multiply into the effective fusion weight,

αeff(t)=α(t)⋅w(t),\alpha_{\text{eff}}^{(t)}=\alpha^{(t)}\cdot w^{(t)}, (8)

which is suppressed whenever either the model does not need help or the caption does not deserve to be trusted. The final logits are a gated residual on top of the clean path,

𝐳final(t)=𝐳clean(t)+αeff(t)​(𝐳cap(t)−𝐳clean(t)),\mathbf{z}_{\text{final}}^{(t)}=\mathbf{z}_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}+\alpha_{\text{eff}}^{(t)}\big(\mathbf{z}_{\text{cap}}^{(t)}-\mathbf{z}_{\text{clean}}^{(t)}\big), (9)

and the next token is yt=arg⁡maxv​𝐳final(t)​(v)y_{t}=\arg\max_{v}\mathbf{z}_{\text{final}}^{(t)}(v). The two paths maintain separate KV caches but share parameters; the selected token is appended to both before the next step. For yes/no and multiple-choice tasks the procedure reduces to a single decoding step on the answer token. GEASS adds two forward passes per query (one for CC, one for 𝐳cap\mathbf{z}_{\text{cap}}), introduces no trainable parameters, and applies to any VLM that exposes decoding logits.

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

Models.

We evaluate GEASS on four VLMs spanning architectures and scales: InternVL2-8B (Chen et al., 2024b), InternVL3-3.8B (Zhu et al., 2025), Qwen2.5-VL-3B (Bai et al., 2025), and Qwen2.5-VL-3B-VLM-R1-Math-305— a reasoning-augmented variant fine-tuned with chain-of-thought supervision, denoted Qwen2.5-VL-3B†. The selection covers standard and reasoning-enhanced architectures of comparable scale.All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU.

Benchmarks.

POPE (Li et al., 2023) probes object existence with binary yes/no questions, reporting accuracy across random, popular, and adversarial sampling. HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024) targets visual illusions and entangled language–vision hallucinations, requiring the model to resist misleading cues.

Baselines.

We compare GEASS against (i) the vanilla model without decoding intervention (Baseline), and (ii) VCD (Leng et al., 2024), a contrastive decoding method that contrasts outputs against a noise-corrupted image. All methods use greedy decoding. GEASS uses fixed hyperparameters τ=0.5\tau{=}0.5, β=10\beta{=}10, η=5\eta{=}5, λ=2\lambda{=}2 throughout, except where stated otherwise.

5.2 Main Results

Table 4 reports POPE and HallusionBench accuracy. GEASS improves over the vanilla baseline on every cell where comparison is available, and surpasses VCD wherever both are reported.

The gain is consistent in scale across models. On POPE, GEASS adds +1.58+1.58 on Qwen2.5-VL-3B (→86.8185.23\!\to\!86.81) and +1.53+1.53 on Qwen2.5-VL-3B† (→86.6885.15\!\to\!86.68), exceeding VCD by +0.86+0.86 on the latter. The gap widens on HallusionBench, where GEASS adds +3.58+3.58 on Qwen2.5-VL-3B† (→64.7761.19\!\to\!64.77) and +2.16+2.16 on InternVL3-3.8B (→68.8766.71\!\to\!68.87), exceeding VCD by +1.58+1.58 where comparable. The asymmetry between the two benchmarks tracks the hypothesis behind GEASS: when the model’s own visual judgment is unreliable—the regime HallusionBench is built to expose—the confidence gate opens more often, and an adaptively gated caption signal has more headroom to contribute. On POPE, where the clean path already produces decisive predictions on most queries, the gate stays mostly closed and GEASS reduces to the baseline by design.

5.3 Effect of Caption Quality

GEASS reads whichever caption it is given; how much do its gains depend on what the caption looks like? Table 5 compares three conditions: None (vanilla baseline), Self (the model’s own caption, our default), and GT (a hand-written description that covers every visible object, attribute, and spatial relation, serving as an upper bound).

The Self setting already captures most of the gain available from caption-aided inference relative to None, even though-as Section 3.4 shows—self-generated captions are dominated by omissions. This indicates that GEASS extracts useful signal from imperfect input rather than depending on perfect captions to function. The Self-vs-GT gap, once measured, quantifies the residual headroom attributable to caption imperfection: a wide gap would suggest that a better captioner could unlock further accuracy, while a narrow gap would indicate that GEASS is already close to the ceiling its reading mechanism allows.

5.4 Hyperparameter Sensitivity

GEASS exposes three hyperparameters beyond the fixed β=10\beta{=}10: the confidence threshold τ\tau, the entropy sensitivity η\eta, and the disagreement penalty λ\lambda. We sweep each on Qwen2.5-VL-3B† / POPE, holding the others at their default.

Table 6 varies τ\tau. A small τ\tau keeps the gate closed unless the model is highly uncertain—safe but conservative. A large τ\tau opens the gate more readily, which raises both correction potential and caption-induced risk. Table 6 sweeps (η,λ)(\eta,\lambda) at fixed τ\tau. As Section 4.3 discusses, the ratio λ/η\lambda/\eta controls the minimum entropy reduction the caption must produce to override a disagreement; a higher ratio favors precision over recall. Across the grid, accuracy stays within a narrow band of the default, indicating that GEASS does not require per-model hyperparameter tuning.

6 Conclusion

We studied how captions influence VLM inference and identified two properties that govern the outcome: a deep anchoring effect, which extends a caption’s influence well past the final answer into the model’s reasoning trajectory, and an asymmetric error structure, in which omission outnumbers fabrication but each fabrication carries a much larger per-instance impact. Because both properties operate on the same caption, mitigating one without the other is not enough.

Acting on this, we proposed GEASS, a training-free module that decides, on each query, how much of the caption the model should consume. GEASS gates the caption by the clean path’s confidence, weights its contribution by the entropy reduction it produces, and raises the evidence bar when the two pathways disagree—a direct encoding of the omission-over-fabrication prior. The mechanism is plug-and-play, adds two forward passes, and applies to any VLM that exposes decoding logits. On POPE and HallusionBench across four models, it improves over vanilla inference and contrastive decoding without per-model tuning.

GEASS treats agreement between the two pathways as evidence of caption reliability, which is correct when fabrications are rare but breaks down when they are not—a regime where the disagreement penalty would suppress a genuine correction. Lifting this assumption, for instance through explicit object-level verification on the caption side, is left to future work.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
